passage:
Monday. Seema stepped off the night bus in Chennai with her bag held in front of her. She asked the auto driver where the guesthouse lane was, then the flower seller, then the man at the tea stall. Two pointed left, one right. She followed the two, and checked once more at the corner shop.
Wednesday. A stranger said, "Come, I'll show you a shortcut." She thanked him, said she would ask at the shop, and did.
Friday. Her colleague Jahnavi laughed at her list of directions. "Three people? Two of them would have done." But the route was correct every time.

qa.q: How many people did Seema ask on Monday for the guesthouse lane?
qa.a: Seema asked the auto driver, the flower seller and the man at the tea stall.

qa.q: What was Seema probably feeling when the stranger offered a shortcut on Wednesday?
qa.a: She was probably cautious and a little uneasy, since she thanked him and chose to check at the shop instead.

qa.q: What did Seema do to reduce the risk of a wrong turn?
qa.a: She asked several people, compared their answers and checked again at the corner shop, keeping her bag in front.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Seema's habit of asking three people?
qa.a: Jahnavi finds it funny and says two would do, but sees that Seema's routes were correct each time.

grounding: Shows a traveller asking several people for directions, checking answers against each other and keeping valuables close over several days.

passage: Beta, I am Mehak, and at twenty-four I travelled to Varanasi with a fellow traveller, Dhruv, who said, "Ask one person, everyone is friendly." Many are, but I asked three people for the way to the ghat: a chaiwala, a shop owner and a woman selling flowers. Two answers matched, and one man who had joined us said he would take us by a different lane. It was longer, and crowded. My bag was zipped and in front of me. At the end of the lane, Dhruv put his hand to his back pocket and found it empty. I checked answers against each other after that, and Dhruv never again trusted a single voice.

qa.q: How many people did Mehak ask for the way to the ghat?
qa.a: Mehak asked three people for the way to the ghat, a chaiwala, a shop owner and a woman selling flowers.

qa.q: What was Mehak probably feeling when a man joined them and offered a different lane?
qa.a: Mehak was probably cautious and alert, since the bag was zipped and held in front and the answers had been checked against each other.

qa.q: What choice by Mehak made the journey safer?
qa.a: Mehak asked several people, checked their answers against each other and kept the bag zipped and in front.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's view of asking for directions have changed after the pocket?
qa.a: Dhruv learned that friendly help is common but one voice may not be enough, and he stopped trusting a single answer.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a traveller who asked several people, compared answers and kept valuables close, against a companion who trusted one voice.

passage: Tushar, twenty-five, got off the bus in a small hill town at dusk with his friend Yamini. His phone had died on the way, and the homestay was somewhere "near the old church". A man at the bus stand offered to walk them there for a fee and reached for Yamini's bag. Tushar gently took it back and kept it on his own shoulder. "We'll manage, thanks." He asked a woman at the fruit stall; she pointed uphill, past the post office. He asked a schoolboy, who said the same. Then a shopkeeper said downhill. Two against one. They went uphill, and at the post office, asked again. The church bell was right there. So was their homestay sign.

qa.q: What was the homestay near?
qa.a: The old church.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt when the man reached for Yamini's bag?
qa.a: He probably felt wary and alert, choosing to take the bag back politely and keep it close.

qa.q: What made Tushar's way of asking for directions reliable?
qa.a: He asked several people, compared their answers, went with the majority and checked again at the post office.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel about the way Tushar handled things?
qa.a: Yamini would likely feel safer and reassured, with the bag kept close and the directions double-checked.

grounding: Shows a traveller with a dead phone asking several locals, checking their answers against each other and keeping bags close.

passage: On her first week in Kolkata for a new job, Vidya, twenty-four, needed to reach an office in Salt Lake from Howrah station. Her phone battery was at five percent. At the station exit, a man said, "Madam, taxi, very cheap, I know the place," and stepped close to her handbag. She moved it to her front and shook her head. She asked a policeman, who told her the bus number. She asked a woman waiting at the stop, who said the same bus and added, "Get off at the water tank." Inside the bus, she asked the conductor to tell her the stop. Her colleague Yusuf, who met her at the office, laughed. "You found it faster than I did in my first week."

qa.q: Where did Vidya need to reach?
qa.a: An office in Salt Lake.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when the man stepped close to her handbag?
qa.a: She felt wary and alert, moving the bag to her front and refusing firmly.

qa.q: Which of Vidya's steps made her journey safe and accurate?
qa.a: She kept her bag close and asked a policeman, a woman at the stop and the conductor, checking each answer against the others.

qa.q: How does Yusuf react to Vidya's arrival?
qa.a: Yusuf is amused and impressed, saying she found it faster than Yusuf did in the first week.

grounding: Shows a traveller asking several people for directions, checking the answers against each other and keeping her bag close.

passage:
Dilnaz: "Ira, the map's no good in these lanes. Let's ask."
Ira: "That boy said left, past the blue gate."
Dilnaz: "Let's check with one more. Bhaiya, which way to the step-well?"
Shopkeeper: "Left, then straight."
Dilnaz: "Two lefts. Good. Keep your phone in your front pocket, na?"
Ira: "Why?"
Dilnaz: "Crowded lane. Just in case."
(A man falls into step beside them.)
Man: "Madam, I'll take you. Special route, very cheap."
Dilnaz: "No, thank you. We know the way."
Ira: "Do we?"
Dilnaz: "We asked two people. That's better than one stranger's special route."
(At the blue gate, they see a signboard: Step-well, 100 metres.)
Ira: "Okay, you're good at this."

qa.q: What was the step-well near, according to the boy?
qa.a: Left, past the blue gate.

qa.q: Why does Dilnaz refuse the man's offer so quickly?
qa.a: Dilnaz feels cautious and alert, preferring checked directions from two people over a stranger's special route.

qa.q: What habits does Dilnaz show that others could copy?
qa.a: Asking more than one person, checking the answers match and keeping valuables in a front pocket in crowded places.

qa.q: How does Ira feel by the time they reach the signboard?
qa.a: Ira feels reassured and a little impressed, admitting Dilnaz is good at this.

grounding: A dialogue shows a traveller asking several locals, checking answers and keeping valuables close while refusing an opportunist.

passage: Looking back on Hanoi, I think the best thing I did was stubborn and boring. I'm Pranav, and on our last evening there, Farida and I had to find the station for the night train to Hue. A man on a scooter pulled up beside us. "Station closed today! I take you to the other station, very fast." He was friendly and completely sure. I thanked him and kept walking. At a pharmacy I showed the woman at the counter our ticket; she pointed straight ahead. "Ten minutes. Open." Two streets on, I asked a hotel receptionist the same question and got the same answer. Two against one. All the while, my passport sat in a pouch under my shirt, and our backpacks were on our fronts through the crowded market street. The station was open, of course. On the train Farida said, "You didn't trust him at all." I said, "I trusted him a third."

qa.q: Where did Pranav first ask for directions after the scooter man?
qa.a: At a pharmacy, from the woman at the counter.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel when the scooter man insisted the station was closed?
qa.a: Pranav felt wary but calm, polite enough to thank him while quietly doubting such a sure and helpful stranger.

qa.q: Why did asking two more people work better than arguing with the scooter man?
qa.a: Two separate locals giving the same answer outweighed one stranger with something to gain, so Pranav could just keep walking.

qa.q: How might Farida have seen Pranav's checking?
qa.a: Farida seems amused and a little impressed, noticing that Pranav didn't take the friendly man at his word.

grounding: Illustrates a traveller who asks several people, checks their answers against each other and keeps valuables close, avoiding an opportunist.
